Blind review: Shared image of air in an embrace: joy in one, pallor in the other.

Blind review: 54 is conditional on firm chastity, so it sits easily beside a fickle-heart simile.
Blind review: A reason for embodiment and a lament that it is temporary fit together.
Blind review: Character shown in deeds and feeling shown on the face do not collide.

Blind review: An enemy's heart may stay unchanged while a prince still makes him an ally.

Adjudicated: Says what rain does, ruining and restoring, not what rain is; a statement of its power is not a definition.
Adjudicated: Speaks of knowing the true nature of the five senses, not of holding them in; restraint has to be read into it.
Adjudicated: About who deserves the name Brahman, a role the Ascetic entry sets apart; nothing in it speaks of renouncing.
Adjudicated: Palanquin bearer and rider illustrate that virtue pays; the couplet shows a case and does not say what the return of deeds is.
Adjudicated: Says love cannot be hidden and tears betray it; a sign of love's presence does not say what love is.
Adjudicated: The point here is the soul's lodging in the body, which the Bones entry excludes and leaves to Soul and Body.
Adjudicated: Worthy and unworthy are known by what they leave behind; this is no test of even-handedness and does not define it.
Adjudicated: A simile for the bond of soul and body; it pictures life's departure and does not say what impermanence is.
Adjudicated: Says inner wit outweighs book learning; even read as destiny it asserts a power and does not say what destiny is.
Adjudicated: The bough tip is the limit of one's reach; the Tree entry pictures what a person is to others, which this is not.
Adjudicated: The flower here only shows how high the water stands; it is not beauty or delicacy, so the watered plant is the image.
Adjudicated: Warns of the disgrace of a slip before the wise; it does not speak of weighing hearers, and that takes more than one step.
Adjudicated: Warns of the sweet words of women who want gold; the man's appetite is not what is judged here.
Adjudicated: The torch here is a futile search under water; it drives out no dark, and is not the lamp used of truth or wealth.
Adjudicated: Names the cause of disease, humours out of balance; it does not say what health or the care of the body is.
Adjudicated: Says high place does not make one high; this denies a false measure and never says what greatness is.
Adjudicated: Ranks farm tasks, manure over ploughing and guarding over watering; it teaches technique and praises nothing about husbandry.
Adjudicated: Explains why begging persists, because some do not refuse; it neither urges giving nor praises it.
Adjudicated: The eye here is only a room to clear for the beloved; it does not act, wound, weep or take blame as the entry says.
Adjudicated: The eye is where he dwells, unhurt by a blink; it is not an actor that fights or suffers as the entry describes.
Adjudicated: The eye is his dwelling, left unpainted so as not to hide him; it is a home, not an actor that wounds or weeps.
Adjudicated: Says the gossip keeps her alive; that is an effect on the speaker, not an account of what gossip is.
He calls the gossip precious, which is praise rather than a definition. Agreed by the build review and the local model.
Adjudicated: The moon here is eclipsed for all to see; none of the entry's moons, waxing, spotted or rivalling her face, is meant.
Adjudicated: A simile for a futile attempt, putting out fire with ghee; it pictures gossip's effect and does not say what gossip is.
Adjudicated: A lover's wry wish that the village keeps talking; nothing here says what gossip is.
Adjudicated: Tears here are plain weeping run dry and proclaim nothing; the working figure is the eyes, not the entry's tears.
Adjudicated: Says the pride of life belongs to those whose love is returned; that is mutual love, not what one-sided love is.
Adjudicated: Tamil has only வேறல்லம், we are not separate; Aiyar adds the one soul, and no soul lodged in a body is pictured.
Adjudicated: A plea to the real moon not to set; it is not waxing, spotted or rivalling her face, so the entry does not apply.
Adjudicated: The bud-to-bloom picture is real, but it shows sickness growing, not the entry's beauty, delicacy or lack.
Adjudicated: The dead of night is only when love rules her heart: a word in its plain sense, not an image.
Adjudicated: Dull eyes and worn fingers are plain signs of waiting; the eyes do not act, fight or take blame here.
Adjudicated: Seeing him to her eyes' content is plain longing; the eyes neither wound nor weep nor take blame.
Adjudicated: The eye that misses the painting brush is plain sight in a simile, not the eye as learning, spies or kindness.

Readings: The ornament isn’t in the Tamil. உறுப்பு means a part, not a jewel.
Readings: There is no ornament or jewel in the Tamil, which says only that it is good if no one can blame it.
Readings: ஏமாப்பு is shelter, not treasure. The image of savings isn’t in the Tamil.
Readings: The Tamil says only that a stone blocks the road of living days. Further births and release are his reading, not its words.
Readings: காட்சி here means understanding. The Tamil has no eye, whole or otherwise.
Readings: The ark isn’t in the Tamil, which says only hold.
Readings: The Tamil says pettiness. Lust comes only from the old note and his gloss.
Readings: Friendship is the old English’s word. The Tamil says cherish them and take them on, and he reads that as helpers.
Readings: The treasure image is the old English’s. The Tamil says a good mind brings prosperity, not that it is the true wealth.
Readings: The ruler is his reading and the old English’s. The Tamil says only those who act.
Readings: The ruler and the campaign are his reading and the old English’s. The Tamil says only those who go on.
Readings: The tank and its channels are the old English’s image. The Tamil says only the way in and the way out.
Readings: The ruler is his reading and the old English’s. The Tamil names no one.
Readings: The kingdom is the old English’s. The Tamil names no ruler and speaks only of the one who does the work.
Readings: The Tamil names no ruler. He supplies one, and the old English follows him.
Readings: The Tamil says justice, not sceptre, so the image isn’t in it.
Readings: The Tamil says only wealth and doesn’t name the ruler. He supplies him, and the old English follows.
Readings: The rod is the old English’s. The Tamil says only raise and strike, and he calls those images.
Readings: The Tamil names no ruler, only someone with a sour face.
Readings: The Tamil names no ruler. He supplies one, and the old English follows him.
Readings: The Tamil has prosperity asking the way, not a goddess. Neither ஆக்கம் nor his gloss, which says wealth, points to Lakshmi.
Readings: The image in the Tamil is a flood, வெள்ளம், not the sea. The sea is the old English.
Readings: The Tamil speaks of firmness in action, not of ambition or great deeds. Aspiration came from the old English.
Readings: The council is the old English. The Tamil names no ruler and no council.
Readings: Rainwater is the old English. The Tamil says water, and he reads it as wells, tanks and rivers that last when the sky fails.
Readings: Vigour is the old English. The Tamil says excellence in action, and he reads it as doing the right work in the right measure, not drive.
Readings: Discipline is the old English. The Tamil says they keep their excellence, and he reads it as fighting on against the ruler’s will.
Readings: The love and the letting pass are the old English. The Tamil speaks of friends acting unasked, not of a friend who has hurt you.

Readings: Seed and sowing aren’t in the Tamil. The image came from the old English.
Readings: The Tamil calls worth a strength, not wealth. The treasure image came from the old English.
Readings: The couplet doesn’t name the family. He supplies it from the chapter, and the old English wrote it in.
Readings: செறாஅர் means those who aren’t hostile, here her friend. “The loving” came from the old English.
Readings: “The lover” came from the old English. The Tamil speaks only of desire, and he reads it as the speaker’s own.
Readings: The Tamil never addresses her friend. “My maid” was the old English, and only his context line brings her in.
Readings: The Tamil says only “I will drink”. The ambrosia is his addition.
Readings: The Tamil praises a woman’s nature, which he reads as simple-mindedness. Reserve came from the old English.
Readings: K488 says carry your enemies, a ruler’s tactic. K963 is about dignity in want. The clash rested on “bow” in both, which the plain K488 doesn’t have.
Readings: The clash needs rebirth in K38 and good deeds among K5’s two kinds. Both are his reading, not the couplets’ words, so the plain readings don’t pull.
Readings: “Hard words” was the old English. K197 lets unjust words pass only to condemn useless ones, and K995 is about scorn. They don’t meet.
Readings: “What pleases him” was the old English. K697 says to say what is wanted and never what is useless, which doesn’t pull against telling him what is good.
Readings: “Enemies should be won over” was the old English. K679 is about those not with you and K879 about clearing a thorn while young: two tactics, no real pull.
Readings: “Two roads to a full life” was the old framing. K342 says nothing of wealth and K760 nothing of renouncing, so they don’t really pull.

Adjudicated: It values closeness as a limb of friendship and urges the worthy to be its salt, which is praise, not definition.

Adjudicated: It is about the striker's joy in a witless, fearful enemy, which is strategy, not a warning against folly.
